newsitem.title: USA: CBOT corn ends sharply lower on funds, weather.
newsitem.headline: CBOT corn ends sharply lower on funds, weather.

text.p: Aggressive fund selling and forecasts for a wet weekend in the U.S. Midwest pushed CBOT corn futures sharply lower for the second day, traders said.
"There is rain in the forecast and there's no heat," said Vic Lespinasse, trader with Dean Witter. "That's a very bearish combination."

Forecasts called for cool weather Tuesday with a gradual warm-up to normal readings seen by Thursday. A weekend storm was expected to bring 0.25 to 1.00 inch of rain to Illinois with 40 to 60 percent coverage, Weather Services Corp said.
But meteorologists disagreed on long-range outlooks with some suggesting a high pressure ridge would move west, opening the door for more moisture to come into the central Corn Belt.

The National Weather Service six- to 10-day outlook, released Monday, also suggested a wetter pattern. NWS called for below normal temperatures and above normal precipitation across much of the U.S. Midwest August 10-14.
But some forecasters predicted dry weather for much of next week with the next chance of rain coming the following weekend.
Corn ended 9-1/4 to 3-3/4 cents per bushel lower with December down 7-3/4 at $2.57-1/4.
Traders noted USDA's weekly crop update showed a modest decline in condition ratings but some had expected a sharper drop after last week's dry weather.
USDA said as of Sunday, U.S. corn was 66 percent good to excellent, below 68 percent the previous week.

"We're seeing more stress (in Iowa) than what we did a week ago," said Dave Maher, analyst with Securities Corp of Iowa. "We've got some areas that are pretty decent. I think there's more stress out there."

However, declines were curbed somewhat by reports Sparks Companies, the Memphis-based private analytical firm, had pegged U.S. corn production at 9.47 billion bushels, below USDA's July outlook for 9.7 billion.
Sparks officials were unavailable for comment on the estimate.
The estimate was released ahead of the August 12 USDA production estimate. Some trade sources said the market was cautious in anticipation of that report.

"Even if there is a weather problem, all the short covering is finished in the market and no wants to take on a big long position into the August 12 crop report," said Charlie Sernatinger, analyst with E D and F Man International. "I think a lot of people bought this stuff on Project A (Sunday) and early Monday and became very unhappy with their position."
The September contract also struggled with reports of increased farmer selling of old crop corn. Cash sources said movement increased on Tuesday despite the sell-off.

On the day, Refco Inc sold at least 17 million bushels December and bought five million, pit sources said. Cargill Investor Services and Rand Financial each sold four million December and Tenco Inc sold five million December.

Commercials were bear spreaders. Cargill Inc spread 2.5 million December/September at two cents, premium December, and Farmers Commodities Corp sporead one million December/September at 2-3/4 cents, traders said.

In options, E.D. and F. Man International bought 600 September $2.70 calls at five cents and sold 600 December $2.40 puts at 4-1/2 cents, floor sources said. ADM sold 400 September $2.50 calls at 10 cents and 400 September $2.50 puts at four cents.
Corn futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 73,000 contracts, compared with Monday's actual volume of 85,897. Options volume was pegged at 25,000 contracts, against Friday's 27,704.
